claims.claim: Bryce Lynch lists boxed text among the things he does not want in an adventure module.
claims.quote: Boxed text is usually not a good thing.

claims.claim: Bryce Lynch names a terse writing style as one of the things he looks for in an adventure module.
claims.quote: Terse writing style

claims.claim: Bryce Lynch says in a comment on his own standards page that he loathes overly long backstory and fiction introductions in modules.
claims.source: Bryce Lynch, comment of 19 April 2016 on 'Review Standards', tenfootpole.org
claims.quote: I LOATHE the overly long backstory

claims.claim: The tenfootpole reviewer who writes as 'The Pretty Girl' puts succinct-and-evocative at the top of her four-point Language scale for modules; the scale is hers, not Bryce Lynch's.
claims.source: 'The Pretty Girl', rating scale on 'Review Standards', tenfootpole.org
claims.quote: 4 – Succinct and evocative
claims.page: Review Standards, 'The Pretty Girl' section, Language scale

claims.claim: Justin Alexander defines boxed text in an RPG scenario as narration written in advance for the GM to read to the players.
claims.quote: a prewritten narration designed to be read to the players

claims.claim: Justin Alexander names the reaction point and says a description must not carry the world past it before the players may respond; he applies the test to a boxed passage he quotes from Journeys Through the Radiant Citadel.
claims.quote: the game world continue to move forward past the reaction point

claims.claim: A commenter on Alexander's post recalls a lost Wizards devblog article arguing GM-delivered descriptive text should stop at three sentences; the recollection is the commenter's, and the original article is not linked.
claims.source: commenter 'mellonbread', comment of 2 August 2022 on The Alexandrian
claims.quote: should never be longer than three sentences
claims.confidence: medium — a reader's memory of an article he says was deleted; unverified against the original

claims.claim: David Noonan reports that from watching games at Gen Con 2005 he concluded a DM reading boxed text holds player attention for two sentences.
claims.source: Jesse Decker and David Noonan, 'Design & Development: Undercover at Gen Con, Part 1', Wizards of the Coast
claims.quote: If you’re the DM, you get two sentences. Period.

claims.claim: Noonan's stated mechanism for the attention loss is that read-aloud text converts the game's normal conversation into oration.
claims.source: Jesse Decker and David Noonan, Wizards of the Coast
claims.quote: Boxed text replaces that conversation with oration.

claims.claim: Noonan sets a three-sentence 2005 boxed text from Sons of Gruumsh beside a much longer one from 1999's Return to the Keep on the Borderlands to show that read-aloud text used to be far longer.
claims.source: Jesse Decker and David Noonan, Wizards of the Coast
claims.quote: Boxed text in adventures used to be a lot longer

claims.claim: Noonan reports that players who heard boxed text still missed its factual content, naming room dimensions, exits and monster counts as what went past them.
claims.source: Jesse Decker and David Noonan, Wizards of the Coast
claims.quote: basic stuff, like room dimensions, how many doors exit the room

claims.claim: The Dungeon Master's Workshop close reading of King Bruenor's speech in Out of the Abyss objects that the passage is formatted like a novel, with a 'he says' attribution tag inside text meant to be spoken.
claims.source: Dungeon Master's Workshop, 'Dungeon Mastering 101: Mastering the Boxed Text'
claims.quote: structuring the narrative like it’s a book
claims.page: section on Out of the Abyss

claims.claim: The same close reading notes that Out of the Abyss's own instruction immediately after the Bruenor boxed text tells the DM to paraphrase it.
claims.source: Dungeon Master's Workshop, quoting Out of the Abyss
claims.quote: Paraphrase Bruenor’s speech as needed
claims.page: section on Out of the Abyss

claims.claim: Dungeon Master's Workshop advises that a boxed text containing a paragraph break is usually already twice as long as it should be.
claims.quote: already too long by half

claims.claim: Dungeon Master's Workshop offers third-person objective and second-person subjective as two switchable registers for the same location description, illustrating each with a waterfall sentence.
claims.quote: A 200-foot waterfall cascades down

claims.claim: Dungeon Master's Workshop reports that Waterdeep: Dragon Heist describes minor locations in mixed forms, a bookstore getting a short paraphrasable paragraph and a villa's great hall a set of bullet points.
claims.quote: A bookstore receives a short paragraph description

claims.claim: James Maliszewski praises the names of Hommlet's inhabitants as Gygax at his best and lists five of them.
claims.quote: are Gygax at his mellifluent best

claims.claim: Maliszewski singles out the holy sayings of St Cuthbert printed in The Village of Hommlet and quotes three of them in capitals as they appear in the module.
claims.quote: his holy sayings presented in the module

claims.claim: Jim Nelson reads Hommlet's villager entries as an iceberg: their ambitions, suspicions and secrets enrich the setting although the players will probably never meet them.
claims.source: Jim Nelson, novelist, 'A different kind of naturalism'
claims.quote: make the setting richer even if little of it is presented

claims.claim: Nelson cites a Hommlet household entry's exact hidden sum as the kind of specific detail that implies a story behind it.
claims.source: Jim Nelson, 'A different kind of naturalism'
claims.quote: stashed seventy-three silver coins in the hollow of a tree

claims.claim: Nelson quotes a reviewer's line that Hommlet is a place whose history shapes its layout, mood and inhabitants.
claims.source: Jim Nelson quoting an unnamed reviewer
claims.quote: is a place with history and its history shapes and affects
claims.confidence: medium — Nelson attributes the sentence only to 'one reviewer' and gives no link

claims.claim: Shawn Merwin's first rule for boxed text is to move from second person to third, and he supplies the same clearing in both, the third-person version making the corpse the subject.
claims.quote: The bloated corpse of a headless dragon dominates the center

claims.claim: Merwin's rule of thumb as a writer and editor is to keep only the environmental details the characters will have to interact with.
claims.quote: leave in only the details about the environment

claims.claim: Merwin's own model opening boxed text, printed in the article, is four sentences and under a hundred words, and he then explains what each of the four sentences does.
claims.source: Shawn Merwin, 'Let's Design an Adventure: Boxed Text', D&D Beyond
claims.quote: Four sentences, and less than 100 words.

claims.claim: Merwin tells adventure writers to avoid 'seems to be' and 'appears to be' in read-aloud text because for the characters perception is reality and the hedge invites metagaming.
claims.quote: For the characters, perception is reality.

claims.claim: Merwin makes reading boxed text aloud a required check, naming tongue-twisters and unintended alliteration as faults invisible on the page.
claims.quote: funny-sounding phrases, unintended alliteration

claims.claim: Merwin tells writers not to use game-mechanical words such as stunned or frightened in their ordinary sense inside read-aloud text.
claims.quote: Avoid game mechanical terms used in a non-mechanical way

claims.claim: Merwin says writing good boxed text needs the precision of fiction or poetry while also doing the work of technical writing.
claims.quote: the same precision that one might use for fiction or poetry

claims.claim: David Hartlage reads the 1989 Gamescience expansion of a Tegel Manor bedroom key as one good middle sentence padded out to length.
claims.quote: pads it like a school paper stretched to an assigned length

claims.claim: Hartlage attributes the padding to the format itself: the custom of long descriptions makes authors write even where they have nothing to add.
claims.quote: encourages authors to write something even when they have little to add

claims.claim: Hartlage argues a location's description should be sized to its purpose in play, instancing a sheriff met about a wanted poster whose kitchen needs no inventory.
claims.quote: no one needs an item-by-item inventory of her kitchen
claims.page: Matching description to a location's purpose

claims.claim: Hartlage says Curse of Strahd gives pages of room description to notable NPCs' homes and calls Chris Perkins's details creepy and moody while judging most of those rooms unreachable in play.
claims.quote: The homes of notable NPCs get pages of room descriptions.
claims.page: Matching description to a location's purpose

claims.claim: Hartlage reports that Curse of Strahd carries boxed text for every location while its successor Storm King's Thunder omits almost all read-aloud text.
claims.quote: omits almost all read-aloud text

claims.claim: Justin Alexander's judgment on the state of the form is that published adventures' location keys are almost all bad.
claims.source: Justin Alexander, 'The Art of the Key', The Alexandrian
claims.quote: the location keys in published adventures are almost universally terrible

claims.claim: Alexander says a standardised section format pushes writers to fill every heading, so a Tactics section gets paragraphs even when the orcs have only swords.
claims.source: Justin Alexander, 'The Art of the Key', The Alexandrian
claims.quote: it tends to encourage writers to “fill the format”

claims.claim: Alexander makes the order of a location description depend on the scene rather than a fixed template, contrasting a visible ogre with a hidden goblin.
claims.source: Justin Alexander, 'The Art of the Key', The Alexandrian
claims.quote: A room with an ogre standing in the middle of it

claims.claim: Alexander dates the arrival of boxed text to Lost Tamoachan and says the prewritten descriptions appeared between quotation marks before TSR boxed them in the 1980 reissue.
claims.source: Justin Alexander, 'The Art of the Key', The Alexandrian
claims.quote: the text was not yet boxed, instead appearing between quotation marks

claims.claim: Bryce Lynch diagnoses Lost Mine of Phandelver's generic feel as a failure of modifiers rather than of nouns and verbs.
claims.source: Bryce Lynch, review of Lost Mine of Phandelver, tenfootpole.org
claims.quote: the adjectives and adverbs were not used very well

claims.claim: Lynch shows the cure as a single added modifier before a role noun and lists six alternatives that would each conjure a different woman.
claims.quote: the prim farmers wife tells you

claims.claim: Lynch's complaint about the Phandalin section is that the town's language is thin outside its core locations.
claims.quote: quite light on descriptive and evocative language

claims.claim: Lynch asks for a web of stated relationships among a town's named residents so the place exists apart from the party.
claims.quote: a web of personal relationships between the various people living in town

claims.claim: Lynch calls the one-sentence-per-NPC summary of who is in town, where they are and what they want invaluable and asks for more adventures to carry one.
claims.quote: That’s done in just a sentence or so each.

claims.claim: Lynch says a monster entry should tell the DM what the characters sense, and offers a smell and a coat as the missing kind of detail.
claims.quote: what the PC’s EXPERIENCE when they meet them

claims.claim: Bryce Lynch calls much of Curse of Strahd's read-aloud laughable and quotes single-sentence examples from it, among them one that names nothing at all.
claims.source: Bryce Lynch, review of Curse of Strahd, tenfootpole.org, quoting Curse of Strahd
claims.quote: You find something on the ground.

claims.claim: Lynch's charge against Curse of Strahd's prose is a fixed inflation ratio, three sentences doing one sentence's work.
claims.quote: Three sentences are used when one will do.

claims.claim: Lynch credits Curse of Strahd with villages whose residents each have something going on, and says events attached to locations are what make the places feel alive.
claims.quote: The villagers and places, in particular, seem more alive

claims.claim: The EN World column's fourth writing step is a halving target for every description, and it names adjectives and adverbs as the writer's enemies.
claims.quote: those words are actually our mortal enemies

claims.claim: The same column argues one well-chosen physical detail can stand for a whole person, instancing the loose skin under an old woman's arm.
claims.quote: it paints a vivid image in your mind of the whole woman

claims.claim: A forum reader rewriting a Bastion of Broken Souls boxed text cuts the phrase 'appears as', calling the hedge a DM reflex the players do not need.
claims.source: forum member 'Dausuul', reply of 15 July 2013 on EN World
claims.quote: "Appears as" is just instinctive DM pedantry

claims.claim: The same reader deletes 'scaly' from the official description on the ground that the noun already carries it.
claims.quote: Scaliness was pure fluff from the start.

claims.claim: Radiating Gnome rewrites an 81-word location description from Dungeon 213 down to 23 words and prints both side by side.
claims.quote: That's 23 words verses the originals 81.

claims.claim: In that rewrite he replaces the causeway's 'rising' with a climbing verb because rising suggests effortless floating.
claims.quote: the ramp needs to climb

claims.claim: He keeps an alliteration on purpose, saying the paired sound will stay in the listener's ear.
claims.quote: which will resonate in the listener's ear
claims.confidence: medium — sits beside Merwin's opposite rule that unintended alliteration is a fault; the two are about intent, not sound

claims.claim: He traces the reader's eye through the original passage from feet to cliff to causeway and back, and moves the load-bearing detail forward because listeners are lost after a sentence or two.
claims.quote: That seems like a lot of redirection

claims.claim: Gus L. holds that plain names in a strange world beat strange names in a familiar one, and reads Lost Mine of Phandelver's invented names as unmemorable.
claims.quote: Simple names used in a way that imply a strange world

claims.claim: Gus L. says the Phandalin locations each get a paragraph and no evocative detail in it.
claims.quote: no evocative detail despite having a paragraph each

claims.claim: Gus L. reads a one-line box of read-aloud text in Lost Mine of Phandelver as a symptom of an outdated house style rather than of that scene.
claims.quote: odd devotion to an antiquated house style

claims.claim: Gus L. calls the Phandalin NPC sidebar useless because it gives a name and a note that the person has a quest and nothing else; Bryce Lynch praises the same device.
claims.quote: a simple list of names with "has a quest for party"

claims.claim: Gus L. contrasts the bare category word for a monster with a specific physical description he writes out, arguing the second makes a mystery of the same creature.
claims.quote: is a mystery to be unraveled

claims.claim: David Hartlage's example of boxed text failing is a 2012 tournament room whose load-bearing runes were listed among unimportant details and missed by his whole team.
claims.source: David Hartlage, 'Picturing the dungeon – boxed text', DMDavid
claims.quote: the text mentioned the runes alongside other, less important details

claims.claim: Hartlage attributes boxed text's drag to delivery: a reader's voice takes a different tone and cadence from speech, and the monotony loses the listener.
claims.quote: their voice takes a different tone and cadence

claims.claim: Hartlage names sunset colour as the type of unimportant ornament too many boxed descriptions dwell on.
claims.quote: the color of the sunset and other bits of obviously unimportant fluff

claims.claim: Hartlage, though he paraphrases at the table, says nothing has replaced boxed text as a way of summarising what players must learn on entering a room.
claims.quote: No one has shown a better way to summarize

claims.claim: Justin Alexander shows the Yawning Portal's first official entry in FR1 Waterdeep and the North was a numbered cross-reference line with no description.
claims.source: Justin Alexander, The Alexandrian, quoting FR1 Waterdeep and the North (1987)
claims.quote: 4. The Yawning Portal (inn) – See Durnan, p. 17

claims.claim: Alexander quotes Ruins of Undermountain (1991) declining to describe the inn on the stated ground of leaving DMs free rein, and calls the claim implausible given three prior books.
claims.source: Justin Alexander quoting TSR's Ruins of Undermountain (1991)
claims.quote: to allow DMs free rein in customizing this rambling, shady place

claims.claim: Alexander records that City of Splendors (1994) fixes the inn's founding year and building class, adding registry-style facts to the accumulated description.
claims.source: Justin Alexander, The Alexandrian, on City of Splendors (1994)
claims.quote: Durnan established the Yawning Portal in 1306 DR.

claims.claim: James Maliszewski characterises pre-1982 module backgrounds as thin and credits Tracy Hickman's modules with introducing NPCs given hopes, dreams and fears.
claims.quote: the thin backgrounds of earlier adventures

claims.claim: Maliszewski quotes The Hidden Shrine of Tamoachan's own DM notes instructing the referee to read the module through and annotate the margins before play.
claims.source: James Maliszewski quoting module C1's Notes for the Dungeon Master
claims.quote: read the module thoroughly before play starts, making notes in the margins
claims.page: Retrospective: The Hidden Shrine of Tamoachan

claims.claim: Bryce Lynch frames published adventure prose as a transfer problem: a private note is only a memory cue, and writing for a stranger must carry the image itself.
claims.quote: The words on the page are only a memory cue

claims.claim: Lynch counts at least two translations between the writer's image and the gamemaster's, and blames dry encounters on their failure.
claims.quote: there are at least two translations between your head and the gamemaster

claims.claim: Alexander's key structure puts the seen-at-a-glance block first and requires it to hold everything conveyed on entering, before checks and before element-by-element detail.
claims.source: Justin Alexander, 'The Art of the Key – Part 2', The Alexandrian
claims.quote: contain all of the information that should be immediately conveyed

claims.claim: Alexander's ordering principle for a location entry is general to specific, tracked against how the reader will actually come by each fact.
claims.quote: move from the general to the specific

claims.claim: The Age of Dusk reviewer's writing standard is that short evocative prose conveys a place's feel and leaves blanks for the GM to fill.
claims.quote: Short, evocative writing communicates the feel of a place

claims.claim: The same standard lists two-page room descriptions among the things everyone dislikes in adventure writing.
claims.quote: room descriptions that go on for two pages

claims.claim: Courtney Campbell's location notation reduces the spoken description to the bolded words alone, everything else waiting on a player's question.
claims.source: Courtney Campbell, 'On Set Design', Hack & Slash
claims.quote: When describing things, I only use the bolded words!

claims.claim: Campbell's stated rule for the same notation is that no unimportant word appears at all.
claims.source: Courtney Campbell, 'On Set Design', Hack & Slash
claims.quote: Any word that is not important, is not used.

claims.claim: A forum reader names the opening boxed text of the Dragonlance series as his favourite worst offender and quotes its first clause.
claims.source: forum member 'delericho', reply on EN World
claims.quote: The air surges fierce and sweet
claims.confidence: medium — a reader's recollection quoted in passing, edition unnamed

claims.claim: A forum reader treats a passage in The Forest Oracle as the standing example of infamously bad boxed text, describing men who are neither tarrying nor running.
claims.quote: the men who are neither tarrying nor running
claims.confidence: medium — allusion, not a transcription of the module's line

claims.claim: Justin Alexander's composition rule for a keyed location is that it must not be a single thing.
claims.source: Justin Alexander, 'Random GM Tip: Awesome Dungeon Rooms', The Alexandrian
claims.quote: avoid having rooms that are just one thing
claims.page: Random GM Tip: Awesome Dungeon Rooms

claims.claim: He puts a number on it: at least three things in the room that reward more than looking.
claims.quote: include at least three interactive elements
claims.page: Random GM Tip: Awesome Dungeon Rooms

claims.claim: Alexander's empty rooms still carry one flavourful feature that leads nowhere, which he distinguishes from barren and featureless.
claims.quote: commonly feature one flavorful thing which does not have a significant interaction

claims.claim: Alexander's habitual repair when prepping a published module is to flag details that are essential but buried mid-paragraph so they are not missed in play.
claims.source: Justin Alexander, 'How to Prep a Module – Part 2', The Alexandrian
claims.quote: essential to the adventure but buried in the middle of a paragraph

claims.claim: Reviewing the 2025 D&D starter set, Alexander finds one action defined differently in the main text and in the glossary of the same book.
claims.source: Justin Alexander, review of Heroes of the Borderlands, The Alexandrian
claims.quote: In the glossary, however, the Influence action is defined

claims.claim: An EN World poster in 2025 recalls a two-sentence ceiling for boxed text and would restrict it to what a character physically senses on entering, plus any creatures.
claims.source: EN World member 'GM Lent', post of 5 April 2025
claims.quote: boxed text shouldn't be more than two sentences

claims.claim: Another poster in the same thread sets the limit at three to five sentences, with further detail held back for players who look closer.
claims.source: EN World moderator emeritus 'el-remmen', post of 5 April 2025
claims.quote: 3 to 5 sentences at most

claims.claim: A poster in the same thread argues for read-aloud prose against the bullet-keyword alternative, saying flat descriptors and boxes of key terms are what he dislikes.
claims.source: EN World member 'Shardstone', post of 5 April 2025
claims.quote: I really hate adventures that have very plain descriptors

claims.claim: A poster prefers vague relative placement in room descriptions over compass directions the characters may not know; another replies that vague placement breaks when the party enters by a different door.
claims.source: EN World members 'Shiroiken' and 'Lanefan', posts of 5 April 2025
claims.quote: I personally dislike the cardinal directions

claims.claim: A poster reports his players want the creatures named before the furnishings, with minor detail held until after the encounter.
claims.source: EN World member 'DragonLancer', quoted at post #39
claims.quote: never mention any monsters or at the very least

claims.claim: A poster avoids read-aloud text because module prose differs from his own speech, so reading it signals to players that the location matters to the plot.
claims.source: EN World member 'humble minion', post of 12 July 2020
claims.quote: the way modules are written is very different

claims.claim: The thread's opening poster, writing from eastern Europe, says reading published text aloud makes the DM sound like a speech synthesiser.
claims.source: EN World member 'oriaxx77', post of 12 July 2020
claims.quote: it turns the DM into a TextToSpeech bot

coverage: Angle roster fetched in full: tenfootpole.org (Review Standards, The Book Introduction, the Phandelver and Curse of Strahd reviews), The Alexandrian (GM Don't List #13, Art of the Key parts 1-2, the Yawning Portal textual history, Awesome Dungeon Rooms, How to Prep a Module 2, the 2025 starter-set review), DMDavid (two posts), Grognardia (three posts), and three EN World forum threads; plus Critical Hits, D&D Beyond, Dungeon Master's Workshop, Dungeon of Signs, Age of Dusk, Hack & Slash and Jim Nelson's site; one primary recovered from the Wayback Machine (Decker and Noonan's 2005 Wizards column, the source the later critics all cite). Not found: Necropraxis "Seen in a Glance" (404; reached only through The Alexandrian's citation). Blocked: no video-essay transcript and no dedicated reading-group thread was reached — WebSearch hit its 200-call session budget early and DuckDuckGo, Marginalia and Reddit all refused direct curl, so late discovery ran on bibliography chasing and site-internal search only. Substantive sources by route: 9 from the named roster, 11 by bibliography chasing and on-site search from those pages, 3 by lateral search before the budget ran out; 27 substantive of 29 fetched, 90 claims, every quotation re-verified verbatim against the fetched text. Full record at scratchpad/prose-research/sweep/found-dnd-close.json with raw notes in find-dnd-close.md.
